The Klagenfurt Cathedral, located in Klagenfurt, Austria (46°37′26″N 14°18′44″E), is a historically and culturally significant religious site originally constructed in 1581 and rebuilt in 1724 after a fire. Initially built by Protestants and dedicated to the Holy Trinity, it was the largest Protestant church in Austria at the time, commissioned by Christoph Windisch, Klagenfurt's first mayor. During the Counter-Reformation in 1600, it was given to the Jesuits and rededicated to Saints Peter and Paul. In 1787, Bishop Franz Xaver von Salm-Reifferscheid designated it as the cathedral of the Diocese of Gurk. The cathedral, also known as Klagenfurter Dom or Dom- und Stadtpfarrkirche Hll. Petrus und Paulus, features Baroque architectural characteristics and serves as the main parish church of Klagenfurt and the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Gurk-Klagenfurt. A parking lot, a railroad track, and a road border the park, with buildings visible beyond the road to the east.  A small rectangular structure is visible in the lower left corner of the park. Falls Park is a public park located in Minnehaha County, South Dakota, United States, situated at 43°33′25″N 96°43′19″W in north central Sioux Falls, covering a physical area of 123 acres (50 ha). The park surrounds the city's waterfalls and features a cafe, an observation tower, and the remains of an old mill, along with the Sioux quartzite barn on its northern edge. The mill, constructed in late 1881, was a seven-story structure built of locally quarried Sioux quartzite, costing nearly $500,000 and capable of processing 1,500 bushels daily, but it closed by 1883 due to inadequate water power and wheat shortages. The barn, owned by the City of Sioux Falls since 1917, initially housed city work animals and now serves as the Stockyards Ag Experience, a museum connecting visitors to agriculture. The park's architectural characteristics highlight its industrial and agricultural history, with cultural significance tied to Sioux Falls' heritage. The cathedral appears as a light-colored, complex structure with a domed roof, located within a dense network of predominantly reddish-brown roofed buildings.  A large, paved, light-colored square is situated in front of the cathedral, and a waterfront with docks and piers is visible to the west.  The surrounding urban area is characterized by narrow streets and a mix of building sizes and shapes. The Cathedral of Syracuse, formally known as the Metropolitan Cathedral of the Most Holy Nativity of Mary, is a historically significant Catholic church located in Syracuse, Sicily, Italy, at coordinates 37.059617°N, 15.293433°E, with its address at Piazza Duomo, Ortygia Island. The current structure dates back to the 7th century, with its façade redesigned in the Sicilian Baroque style between 1725 and 1753. Originally a Greek Doric temple built in the 6th century BC, it was converted into a cathedral by Saint Bishop Zosimo of Syracuse, later transformed into a mosque in 878 during Arab rule, and reconverted to a cathedral in 1086 after the Norman conquest. The cathedral's architectural characteristics reflect a blend of Greek Doric columns, Norman mosaics, and Sicilian Baroque elements, including a façade designed by Andrea Palma with Corinthian columns and statues by Ignazio Marabitti. Its interior features a nave and two aisles with Baroque details, a 12th or 13th-century marble font, and a statue of the Madonna della Neve by Antonello Gagini. The cathedral holds relics of St. Lucy and is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site designated in 2005, recognized for its architectural and cultural significance. Major events in its history include its conversion to a mosque in 878, reconversion to a cathedral in 1086, the Baroque façade redesign (1725–1753), and its UNESCO inscription in 2005. This is a remote sensing image of La Fortaleza. The image shows a collection of buildings with light-colored roofs clustered around a large rectangular green field and a nearby larger building, interconnected by visible dirt tracks or roads. This settlement is situated within a dense area of green vegetation and bordered by forested areas. La Fortaleza, a government building located in Old San Juan, San Juan, Puerto Rico (63 Calle Fortaleza, San Juan, Puerto Rico 00901), also known as the Palacio de Santa Catalina, is the official residence and workplace of the governor of Puerto Rico and the oldest executive mansion in continuous use in the New World.  Its construction period spanned from 1533 to 1540 under the orders of King Charles I of Spain, serving as the first fortification on San Juan Islet to defend San Juan Bay.  Designated a World Heritage Site in 1983, La Fortaleza's historical background includes major events such as the Battles of San Juan in 1595, 1598, 1625, and 1797, the Bombardment of San Juan in 1898, the 1950 San Juan Nationalist revolt (an attempted attack on then-governor Luis Muñoz Marín resulting in four Nationalist deaths and three injured guards), its designation as a United States National Historic Landmark in 1960, and its declaration as a World Heritage Site in 1983.  Architecturally, the complex displays Fortification, Spanish Renaissance, and Neoclassical styles, comprising attached buildings with formal living quarters on the second floor and private quarters on the third, along with the Astral Tower and the Homenaje Tower (housing the Santa Catalina Chapel with a 95,000-piece mosaic honoring the Holy Trinity).  Its cultural significance stems from its continuous use as the Governor's residence since the 16th century. Notable visitors include Herbert Hoover, Harry S. Truman, John F. Kennedy, Barack Obama, and Bill Clinton.  Details include the two towers signifying its military origins, the chapel mosaic, the discovery of a possible old kitchen in the Austral Tower in 1956, paintings on loan from the Institute of Puerto Rican Historical Culture, original salmon red paint (characteristic of Spanish colonial military installations), green wooden doors, white and gold columns, and the flying of the Puerto Rican, American, and Governor's flags. The Hundido Garden, renamed Doña Inés Garden after Governor Luis Muñoz Marín's wife, was her favorite spot. The museum complex appears as a collection of interconnected, mostly rectangular buildings with varying roof colors (red, beige, and gray) surrounded by green spaces and trees.  A circular structure is visible within the museum grounds, and roads border the complex on multiple sides, connecting to a larger urban area with other buildings and paved surfaces. The National Museum of Ghana, located at 5°33′37.5″N 0°12′23.1″W in Greater Accra with the address 2 Barnes Road, Accra, is the largest and oldest of the six museums under the Ghana Museums and Monuments Board (GMMB). Established in 1957, it originated from the anthropology museum at Achimota College, founded by Charles Thurstan Shaw, and its collection was later donated to the University of Ghana in 1940. The museum opened on 5 March 1957 as part of Ghana's independence celebrations, with Princess Marina performing the official opening. It closed in 2015 for restoration and reopened in 2022. The structure, built by the Gold Coast Public Works Department with British architects Denys Lasdun and Lindsay Drake, features concrete construction with windows set in saw-toothed angles and a low saucer-shaped aluminium dome. Culturally significant as part of Nkrumah's campaign to foster nationalism, the museum houses approximately 10,000+ objects, including archaeology, ethnography, and fine art, with a focus on Akan origin and African history. Notable visitors include Princess Marina, and the museum also features a library, conservation laboratory, and education hall, with exhibits on the transatlantic slave trade added in the 1990s. This is a remote sensing image of Warta Mouth National Park.  A cluster of buildings with reddish-brown roofs is visible near a road, surrounded by green vegetation and open areas. A body of water is partially visible in the top right corner, separated from the buildings by the road and a band of trees. Several smaller waterways or ditches meander through the predominantly green landscape. The Warta Mouth National Park, located in the Lubusz Voivodeship, Poland, at coordinates 52°34′37.92″N 14°43′32.88″E near Chyrzyno, Kostrzyn nad Odrą, spans a physical area of 80.38 km² and is the youngest of Poland's 23 national parks, established on 19 June 2001. It was created in the region of the lowest stretch of the Warta River, up to its confluence with the Odra (Oder), marking the Polish–German border, and incorporates the former Słońsk Nature Reserve (established in 1977) and parts of the Ujście Warty Landscape Park. Designated under the Ramsar Convention in 1984, the park protects swampy and muddy grounds that serve as a critical haven for birds. Major events in its history include the establishment of the Słońsk Nature Reserve in 1977, its Ramsar designation in 1984, and the official creation of the national park in 2001. Culturally and ecologically significant, the park safeguards 245 bird species, including endangered ones, and plays a vital role in conserving Europe's increasingly rare wetland ecosystems. The park is divided into two parts by the Warta River: the Southern part, which includes the former Słońsk reserve and acts as a seasonal lake with water levels rising up to four meters annually, and the Northern Polder, rich in canals and separated from the Warta by a levee. The ecosystem faces threats from regrowing vegetation in meadows and pastures, endangering bird habitats. The park's Board manages a lodge and guest-house, along with walking and cycling trails and nature walks through the Słońsk reserve. Since 1996, the Centre of Natural Education in Chyrzno has organized educational activities like trips, ornithology camps, and ecology workshops. This is a remote sensing image of Dieng Plateau. A dense cluster of buildings with dark gray and reddish-brown roofs is centrally located, surrounded by a patchwork of agricultural fields in varying shades of green and brown. A light-colored road traverses the image, passing through the agricultural areas and bordering the more densely populated area.  Several covered structures, likely greenhouses or agricultural buildings, are interspersed among the fields. The Dieng Plateau, a historic site categorized as a religious site and place of worship, is located in Central Java, Indonesia, specifically at 7°12′S 109°54′E within Banjarnegara Regency and Wonosobo Regency. Its physical area spans approximately 6 km north to south and 14 km west to east. Constructed between the 8th and 9th centuries, the Dieng Plateau is renowned for its ancient Hindu temples from the Mataram Kingdom era, serving as a significant religious center for Hinduism, especially for the worship of Shiva. Its name, derived from Old Javanese, translates to 'place of the ancestors' or 'place where the gods reside.'  Historically, Thomas Stamford Raffles documented around 400 ancient temples and archaeological sites in 1815. J. Kinsbergen reactivated the Gangsiran Aswatama water channel and excavated several archaeological remains in 1856. From 1911 to 1916, H. L. Melville's research documented 104 archaeological findings. The temples, influenced by South Indian architecture, are clustered into Arjuna, Dwarawati, and Gatotkaca groups, with the Bima temple standing alone.  These structures, primarily dedicated to Shiva, feature phallus, yoni, statues, and inscriptions. Culturally significant as a former Hindu religious center, its high elevation and fertile land connected the earth and the divine.  Notable visitors include Raffles, H.C. Cornelius, Kinsbergen, and Melville. The plateau, the highest in Java at over 2,100 meters above sea level, experiences a cold climate, including Bun Upas (freezing temperatures), and is a major potato producer with geothermal energy resources. The Ming tombs, a Historic Site located in Changping District, Beijing Municipality, China (40°15′12″N 116°13′3″E), specifically in the suburban Changping District, 42 kilometers north-northwest of Beijing's city center, occupy a physical area of 40 km² (15 sq mi).  Construction began in 1420 onwards. Historically, the Ming tombs are a collection of mausoleums built by the Ming dynasty emperors. Most are clustered near Beijing, collectively known as the Thirteen Tombs of the Ming dynasty. The third Ming emperor, the Yongle Emperor, chose the site based on feng shui principles. Thirteen Ming emperors were buried there.  Li Zicheng's army ransacked and burned the tombs in 1644. In 1725, the Yongzheng Emperor bestowed the hereditary title of marquis on a Ming imperial descendant to perform rituals at the tombs. Major events include the Imperial Palace (Forbidden City) construction in 1420, after which the Yongle Emperor selected his burial site and created his mausoleum; the ransacking and burning of the tombs by Li Zicheng's army in 1644 before capturing Beijing; and the UNESCO World Heritage Site inscription in August 2003 under the 'Imperial Tombs of the Ming and Qing Dynasties' designation.  Architecturally, the tombs follow Feng Shui principles within an arc-shaped valley at the foot of the Jundu Mountains. A 7-kilometer 'Spirit Way' leads into the complex, lined with statues. The 'Great Red Gate', a three-arched red painted gate, serves as the front gate. The Spirit Way begins with a huge stone memorial archway, among China's largest.  A 50-ton Bixi statue carrying a memorial tablet and four white marble Huabiao (pillars of glory) mark the stele pavilion. Eighteen pairs of mythical animal stone statues lead to the Dragon and Phoenix Gate, a three-arched gate. Culturally, the tombs represent the burial sites of Ming dynasty emperors, reflecting当时的 architectural and cultural practices, and their UNESCO World Heritage Site status highlights their global significance. Primarily, they functioned as imperial mausoleums.  The Ming tombs are part of the 'Imperial Tombs of the Ming and Qing Dynasties' World Heritage Site, including other locations near Beijing and in Nanjing, Hebei, Hubei, and Liaoning provinces. Only three tombs are open to the public, with no excavations since 1989, but plans for new research and further openings exist. This is a remote sensing image of Wrigley Mansion. The mansion, with its reddish-brown roof and multi-tiered structure, is situated amidst sparse desert vegetation, near a marina filled with boats on a segment of the Arizona Canal.  Residential areas with white-roofed buildings and swimming pools are visible to the northwest and southeast, while larger, gray-roofed commercial structures are located across the canal to the north. The Wrigley Mansion, categorized as a Mansion, is located in Phoenix, Arizona at 33°31′21.74″N 112°1′33.61″W ﻿ / ﻿ 33.5227056°N 112.0260028°W ﻿ / 33.5227056; -112.0260028 (33.52270556 latitude, -112.0260028 longitude), with the address 2501 E. Telawa Trail.  The mansion, exceeding 16,000 square feet (1,500 m²) with 24 rooms and 12 bathrooms, was constructed between 1929 and 1931 by William Wrigley Jr.  Known as both the William Wrigley Jr. Winter Cottage and La Colina Solana, it was designed by architect Earl Heitschmidt in Mission/Spanish Revival and Spanish Colonial styles, featuring extensive tilework from Wrigley's Catalina factory.  Wrigley died in 1932 shortly after its completion.  In 1989, the mansion was added to the National Register of Historic Places, and in 1992, Geordie Hormel purchased it, making it available for meetings and conventions.  It is a designated Phoenix Point of Pride and represents Wrigley's legacy as a historical and architectural landmark.  Currently, it functions as a private club for meetings, conventions, and events. Primarily inhabited by the Nakhi people, whose subsistence relies on grain production and hiking tourism, the gorge holds immense cultural significance as one of the world's deepest and most spectacular river canyons. Sani Pass, a bridge located in the Drakensberg Mountains on the border of KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, and Mokhotlong, Lesotho, stretches approximately 9 km along the road between Himeville and Mokhotlong.  Historically used by the San and Bantu peoples to traverse the Drakensberg, the pass saw initial development in 1922 with a pack animal track, followed by jeep transport from 1949 and tourist access from 1956. Improvements were made in 1958, and the Mokhotlong Mountain Transport Company continued operations after the previous business concluded.  Major events include the first Roof of Africa Rally in 1966, organized by the Sports Car Club and sponsored by The Star newspaper; Phase 1 of the Sani Pass upgrade from 2006-2012; Phase 2 approval in 2013 by the South African Department of Environmental Affairs and Tourism; and the 2014 announcement of Phase 2 tarring by the South African Environmental Affairs Minister. The pass, characterized by its steep gravel road with gradients up to 1:3, experiences frequent snow and ice in winter. Ongoing upgrades include improved storm-water drainage and retaining walls.  Culturally significant as a historical route and a vital transportation link, Sani Pass is a popular tourist destination for adventure drives. The monument, a square, tan-colored structure, sits within a circular, paved area surrounded by a low wall, located near a complex of buildings with paved parking areas. Constructed between 1937 and 1949, its historical background lies in commemorating the Voortrekkers who departed the Cape Colony between 1835 and 1854.  The monument's conception dates back to 1888, with construction commencing in 1937 marked by a sod-turning ceremony performed by Advocate Ernest George Jansen. In 1938, descendants of Voortrekker leaders laid the cornerstone, and Prime Minister D. F. Malan inaugurated the monument in 1949. It achieved National Heritage Site status in 2011, declared by the South African Heritage Resource Agency.  This granite structure, featuring a 40x40 meter square base, houses the world's largest marble Historical Frieze within its domed Hall of Heroes, depicting the Great Trek. Its Cenotaph Hall's cenotaph is uniquely illuminated by sunlight annually on December 16th. The monument exhibits European architectural influences akin to the Dôme des Invalides and the Völkerschlachtdenkmal, yet integrates African elements as well.  A potent symbol of Afrikaner heritage and nationalism, the monument embodies the Great Trek's hardships and the Battle of Blood River and Day of the Vow. It showcases a fusion of European and African cultural and architectural influences, primarily serving as a commemorative monument and historical site. Notable figures like Paul Kruger and D. F. Malan have visited the monument, which further includes a 20,000-seat amphitheatre, a 64-granite ox-wagon laager, a bronze Voortrekker family sculpture, and statues of Voortrekker leaders Piet Retief, Andries Pretorius, Hendrik Potgieter, and an unknown leader. The Trezzo sull'Adda Bridge, categorized as a bridge located in Lombardy, Italy (45°36′42″N 9°31′20″E / 45.61167°N 9.52222°E / 45.61167; 9.52222), specifically Trezzo sull'Adda, Capriate San Gervasio, was constructed between 1370 and 1377.  Historically, this bridge, commissioned by Bernabò Visconti, lord of Milan, held the record for the largest span for over four centuries until the Industrial Age.  Fortified with towers, it provided access to the Visconti Castle and ultimately collapsed in 1416 during a siege.  Key events include its construction in 1377 under Bernabò Visconti and its collapse in 1416 when condottiero Carmagnola deliberately weakened one of its abutments during a siege.  Architecturally, the single-arch sandstone bridge spanned 72 meters (236 ft) with a width of 9 meters (30 ft), featuring a segmental arch with a span-to-rise ratio of 3.3:1 and a rib thickness to clear span ratio of 1/32.  Culturally significant as a testament to medieval engineering and strategic bridge importance, its primary function was to facilitate pedestrian, horse, cart, and wagon traffic across the Adda River while also supporting the Visconti Castle. A roughly trapezoidal area of light brown, appearing as excavated earth and some low stone walls, is surrounded by green vegetation and sits adjacent to a curving paved road. Nebet Tepe, a Historic Site located in Plovdiv, Bulgaria at 42°09′04″N 24°45′08″E ﻿ / ﻿ 42.151236°N 24.752182°E ﻿ / 42.151236; 24.752182 (42.1512299 latitude, 24.7522488 longitude),  with the address Plovdiv, Bulgaria,  dates back to the 4th century BC.  Its historical background reveals its significance as one of the founding hills of ancient Plovdiv, with initial Thracian settlements around 4000 BC, followed by expansions led by Philip II of Macedon and the Roman Empire.  Nebet Tepe served as the citadel of the town's acropolis, evidenced by remnants of walls, towers, and a postern from Justinian's era leading to the Maritsa river.  Major historical events include Thracian settlement (4000 BC), expansion by Philip II of Macedon (4th century BC), Roman Empire expansion (1st century AD), and the postern's construction (6th century AD).  Architecturally, the site displays cyclopean masonry from the 4th century BC, Hellenistic period features like the Western wall and its quadrangular tower, later period walls, and a unique Roman postern with a staircase and a secret tunnel built during Justinian's reign.  Water reservoirs, including a large 350 m3 rectangular one, are preserved on the hill. Culturally, Nebet Tepe, meaning "The hill of the guards" (from Turkish "nevbet" - guard, "tepe" - hill), holds national significance as a popular tourist attraction. Tell el-Dab'a, a historic site in the Nile Delta, Egypt (30°47′N 31°50′E ﻿ / ﻿ 30.783°N 31.833°E ﻿ / 30.783; 31.833), located in Sharqia, is the modern name for the ancient city of Avaris, the Hyksos capital. Tell el-Dab'a boasts a rich history, having been occupied by Asiatics and developing into a large city blending Near Eastern and Egyptian cultures.  It served as a military rival to the Egyptians until its defeat and partial abandonment at the end of the Second Intermediate Period, with full abandonment following the construction of Pi-Ramesses under Ramesses II.  Key events in its history include the initial excavation by Édouard Naville in 1885, excavations by Pierre Montent in 1929 and 1939 20km north (mistakenly believed to be Avaris), its rediscovery by Labib Habachi (1941-1942) confirming it as Avaris, detailed studies by Manfred Bietak in the 1980s solidifying this hypothesis and revealing its status as the Hyksos capital, and a documented epidemic in 1715 BC.  The site's architecture combines Egyptian and Canaanite styles, evident in residences, tombs, and temples oriented NNW-SSE with entrances in the north wall. Temple I, built in the Egyptian style, features three sanctuaries and evidence of an altar, while Minoan wall paintings showcase characteristic Minoan fresco techniques and themes. Tell el-Dab'a's cultural significance lies in its representation of cultural exchange between Near Eastern and Egyptian societies, its role as the Hyksos capital, and its insights into burial practices, trade (evidenced by Cypriot pottery), and artistic influences.  Notable figures associated with the site include Édouard Naville, Pierre Montent, Labib Habachi, Manfred Bietak, and Irene Forstner-Müller.  The site's society interacted with individuals from other regions, influencing their frescos, and engaged in trade with Cyprus. The Hyksos citadel was built towards the end of the Hyksos Period, and the New Kingdom's weighing system may have originated from the shekel system used at Tell el-Dab'a. Nearby Ezbet Rushdi houses a Middle Kingdom temple and settlement. This tropical and subtropical moist broadleaf forest ecoregion extends from southern Bolivia into northern Argentina, occurring at elevations ranging from 800 to 3,000 meters (2,600 to 9,800 feet). Known for its rich biodiversity, the region serves as a critical habitat for unique and endangered species and acts as a transition zone between different ecological regions, thus holding significant cultural importance. With a subtropical highland climate, the Yungas experiences up to 2,500 mm (98 in) of rainfall annually, with a dry season extending from April to October and occasional snowfall at higher elevations during winter. The area can be divided into several elevation zones. Foothill forests are found between 400 to 900 meters, receiving 550 to 1,400 mm of rainfall annually (mean 820 mm), with temperatures averaging 21.5°C (maximum 27.6°C, minimum 15.4°C). Montane forests, at elevations of 900 to 1,600 meters, receive 1,100 to 2,300 mm of rainfall annually (mean 1,800 mm), with an average temperature of 11.7°C (highest 21.8°C, lowest 8.8°C). Upper montane forests, from 1,600 to 2,300 meters, receive 800 to 1,400 mm of rainfall annually (mean 1,100 mm), with the same temperature range as montane forests. The flora in the foothill forests is dominated by Leguminosae, which are largely dry-season deciduous. Montane forests showcase a diversity including Leguminosae, Sapindaceae, Lauraceae, Euphorbiaceae, and Myrtaceae, while upper montane forests contain species like Andean alder (Alnus acuminata), Podocarpus parlatorei, and queñoa (Polylepis australis). Fauna includes mammals such as the red brocket (Mazama americana), gray brocket (Mazama gouazoupira), white-lipped peccary (Tayassu pecari), collared peccary (Dicotyles tajacu), South American tapir (Tapirus terrestris), jaguar (Panthera onca), puma (Puma concolor), margay (Leopardus wiedii), and jaguarundi (Herpailurus yagouaroundi). Winnington Hall is a Grade I listed mansion located in Cheshire, England, at coordinates 53°16′07″N 2°32′01″W, with an address in Winnington, Northwich. The site spans 600 acres (240 ha) and features a rich historical background, originally constructed as a timber-framed house in the late 16th or early 17th century for the Warburton family, with a stone extension added in 1775 by Richard Pennant, 1st Baron Penrhyn, designed by Samuel Wyatt. The hall served as a girls' finishing school in the 19th century, attracting notable figures like John Ruskin and Edward Burne-Jones, and was later purchased in 1872 by industrialists John Brunner and Ludwig Mond for industrial use. After World War I, it was converted into the Winnington Hall Club for Brunner Mond staff, and in 1920, it was restored by Darcy Braddell, with much of its current interior decoration dating from this period. Architecturally, the hall comprises an older timber-framed oak wing with plaster-filled panels and chevrons and a newer stone wing with Neoclassical elements, sash windows, and canted ends, featuring rooms like the Stone Hall, Oak Room, and Orangery. Culturally significant, it reflects the evolution of English country houses and is now used as office space, divided into over 40 offices as of 2011. The Cardamom Mountains, or Krâvanh Mountains, a historic site located in southwest Cambodia and Eastern Thailand (12°00′N 103°15′E),  stretch 300 km (190 mi) NW/SE and 70 km (43 mi) NE/SW.  These mountains, featuring dense tropical rainforests, unique wildlife, and historic sites from the 15th-17th centuries including jar burials and rock art, served as a Khmer Rouge stronghold during the 1970s Cambodian-Vietnamese War before being driven out by Vietnamese forces.  In 2016, the southern slopes were designated as a national park to protect the region's biodiversity.  Culturally significant for their unique jar burials (containing ceramic jars and log coffins representing a previously unrecorded burial practice in Khmer culture), rock art in Kanam Cave (depicting ancient elephants, deer, and wild cows reflecting the region's ecological and cultural history), the mountains are a natural and historic site home to diverse ecosystems, including tropical rainforests, offering refuge to endangered species such as Asian elephants, Siamese crocodiles, and clouded leopards.  Indigenous groups like the Chhong and Por inhabit the region, which faces threats from illegal logging, poaching, and infrastructure projects despite conservation efforts, with community-based ecotourism emerging in villages like Chi Phat.
